blocks.text: This topic covers JSON payloads at the transport encoding level, converting a native data structure to a JSON string and back, escaping special characters correctly, handling nested structures, and payload size limits, distinct from JSON generation, covered in an earlier module, which was about the model producing JSON as its actual response content.
This topic covers encoding and decoding JSON, correctly escaping special characters, working with nested objects and arrays, handling non-ASCII characters, and practical payload size limits.
1. JSON as the Universal Transport Format

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: Building on status codes, JSON payloads cover the transport encoding itself

blocks.text: This topic covers JSON specifically as the serialization format carrying a request or response body over the wire, converting your application own native data structures into the JSON text format actually sent over HTTP, and back again on the receiving end.
2. Encoding, Native Structure to JSON String

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A native data structure gets encoded into a JSON string

blocks.text: Encoding converts a native data structure in your programming language, a dictionary, a list, into the actual JSON text format that gets sent as the request body, this connects directly to the request body topic covered earlier in this module, virtually every programming language has a standard library for this exact conversion.
3. Decoding, JSON String Back to Native Structure

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A received JSON string gets decoded back into a native data structure

blocks.text: Decoding reverses this process, taking the raw JSON text a provider actually returns and converting it back into a native data structure your application can work with directly, this connects directly to the response body topic covered earlier in this module.

code.content:
response_data = json.loads(raw_response_text)  # decoding: JSON text back to native structure
content = response_data["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]

blocks.text: 4. Escaping Special Characters

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: An unescaped quote inside a string value breaks JSON parsing

blocks.text: A string value inside JSON containing a literal quote character, or certain other special characters, needs proper escaping to remain valid JSON, this is exactly why building a payload programmatically and using a standard library encoder, rather than hand-assembling a JSON string, matters, the library handles this escaping correctly and automatically every time.

blocks.text: 5. Nested Objects and Arrays

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A nested object and a nested array can both nest to arbitrary depth

blocks.text: JSON supports objects and arrays nesting inside each other to arbitrary depth, this connects directly to the messages array structure covered in the request body topic, and to nested JSON structures covered in the earlier JSON Generation module, working correctly with deeply nested payloads requires the same standard library tools, not manual string manipulation.
6. Character Encoding and Unicode

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A non-ASCII character gets properly encoded as Unicode

blocks.text: This connects directly to tokens and tokenization, covered in an earlier module, a prompt or response containing non-English characters, emoji, or other non-ASCII content needs to be properly encoded as Unicode within the JSON payload, standard library JSON encoders handle this correctly by default, a hand-rolled encoding approach risks corrupting this content.

blocks.title: This matters more than it might first appear for international applications
blocks.content: An application serving users across different languages needs this Unicode handling to work correctly for every request, a subtle encoding bug here can silently corrupt non-English text in ways that are easy to miss during testing with only English content.

blocks.text: 7. Payload Size Limits

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A very large payload may exceed a provider size limit

blocks.text: This connects directly to context window optimization, covered in an earlier module, a genuinely very large payload, an extremely long conversation history or an oversized document included as context, can exceed a provider maximum accepted request size, independent of the model own context window limit, worth checking a specific provider documentation for this separate constraint.
8. Common JSON Serialization Bugs

Bugs at this transport layer typically stem from bypassing standard library encoding and decoding tools, manually concatenating strings to build JSON, or writing custom parsing logic instead of using a proven JSON library, both invite subtle, hard to diagnose bugs that a standard library would have prevented entirely.
9. JSON Payloads vs the Model Generating JSON

This topic is worth distinguishing clearly from JSON generation, covered in an earlier module, that topic covered getting a model to produce JSON as its actual response content, this topic covers the separate, lower level concern of how the request and response themselves get encoded and transmitted as JSON over HTTP, regardless of what the model actual content happens to be.
Worked Example

A developer manually concatenating strings to build a JSON request body encounters a bug when a user message happens to contain a quote character, the resulting malformed JSON causes the entire request to fail with a confusing parse error on the provider side.

Switching to a standard library JSON encoder to build the request body eliminates this bug entirely, the library automatically and correctly escapes the quote character, along with any other special character that might appear in future user messages, without any additional code needed.
Common Mistakes

items: Manually concatenating strings to build JSON instead of using a standard library encoder
Writing custom JSON parsing logic instead of using a proven, standard library decoder
Not accounting for a provider maximum payload size limit, separate from the model context window limit
Assuming Unicode and non-English content will be handled correctly without verifying it against a standard library encoder

blocks.text: Practice

Take a data structure containing a nested object, an array, and a string value that includes a quote character, encode it to JSON using your programming language standard library, decode it back, and confirm the quote character survives the round trip correctly.
Key Takeaway

JSON payloads are the actual transport encoding carrying a request or response body over HTTP, encoding and decoding this correctly, including proper escaping, nested structures, and Unicode handling, is best left entirely to a standard library rather than hand-rolled string manipulation, and this transport level concern is distinct from the model itself generating JSON as its actual response content, covered in an earlier module.
